source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments? (arXiv v1 PDF, Tables 3 and 4)
finding: Gap 9 resolved. The 0.755 and 0.771 figures are both in the same paper but in two different tables. Table 3 (in-context) lists prior systems Ai and Tu 0.771 F1 and KAF-SPA 0.813. Table 4 (fine-tuning) lists prior best Ai and Tu 0.755, AGED 0.751, KAF-SPA 0.751. The +3.0 and +3.9 F1 claim is against 0.755.
numbers: Table 3 ICL: GPT-4o-mini F1 0.471 (P .416, R .543, acc .308); DeepSeek V3 0.548; GPT-4o 0.592; KID 0.756; AGED 0.767; Ai and Tu 0.771; KAF-SPA 0.813. Table 4 fine-tuned: Qwen 2.5-7B 0.762, GPT-4o-mini 0.768 (fine-tuned), Phi-4 0.785, Qwen 2.5-72B 0.794 vs Ai and Tu 0.755 (+3.0 and +3.9).
quote: surpassed the previous best-performing system Ai and Tu (2024) by +3.0% and +3.9% F1 score
limits: Table 3 and Table 4 rows for prior systems differ (0.771 vs 0.755 for the same system), so they probably use different evaluation settings; the paper text I read does not explain this. Earlier a20/c01 mixed the two tables.
agent_relevance: Quote the +3.9 gain only as 'fine-tuned Qwen 72B vs 0.755'. The ICL numbers (0.47-0.59) are far below supervised, so role filling stays the weak step.

finding: Only one arXiv version exists (submitted 18 Feb 2025). Requests for v2, v3 and v4 HTML pages return 404. So no later arXiv version with different numbers exists. An EMNLP 2025 version exists (aclanthology emnlp-main.1557) and was not opened.
numbers: arXiv HTML v2/v3/v4: HTTP 404 each. Abstract page shows [v1] only.
limits: The EMNLP camera-ready may differ from the arXiv text; not opened.
agent_relevance: Use the v1 numbers with the table labels in d01.

source: Vijayvargiya, Zhou, Yerukola, Sap, Neubig (2026) Ambig-SWE (ICLR 2026, arXiv v3), RQ2 detection
finding: Detection of underspecified tasks is weak and prompt-sensitive. Models almost never ask unless told to. Only Claude Sonnet 4 reaches good accuracy, and only with the strongest prompt. Detection was tested by mixing fully specified and underspecified SWE-bench Verified issues.
quote: models, except Claude Sonnet, fail to reliably distinguish them
limits: Models are 2025-era (Sonnet 4, Qwen 3 Coder). 500 SWE-bench Verified issues, but Sonnet 4 in the Hidden setting only on 100. Detection is judged by whether the model chose to interact.
agent_relevance: A bare 'ask if unclear' instruction is not a reliable missing-role detector. Expect a false-positive cost: Sonnet 3.5 moderate prompt FPR .24 and Llama FPR .93. Any missing-role step needs a check on both error types.

source: Vijayvargiya et al. (2026) Ambig-SWE, RQ1 and RQ3 (interaction value and cost)
finding: Interaction recovers much of the performance lost to missing information, but it costs steps, and it helps only if the question is the right kind. Gains are up to 74% over non-interactive. Sonnet 3.5 and Haiku 3.5 recover up to 80% of the Full-setting score, Sonnet 4 reaches 89%, DeepSeek 59%, Llama 54%.
numbers: Sonnet 4 steps rise 65 to 75 with interaction; Qwen 3 Coder 65 to 65. Navigational info (file paths) asked in 9.0% (Sonnet 3.5) to 30.7% (DeepSeek) of issues. Resolve with vs without navigational info: Sonnet 4 67.2 vs 60.8; Qwen 3 Coder 52.4 vs 55.4 (worse with it); Sonnet 3.5 59.5 vs 37.9; Haiku 36.9 vs 24.8; DeepSeek 13.2 vs 4.6; Llama 6.3 vs 4.3.
limits: Simulated user. Interaction gap to Full stays significant for all models. Some Hidden-setting scores may be inflated by memorised fixes (the paper says possible data leakage).
agent_relevance: Asking what the task is meant to do (informational) is the useful part; asking for facts the agent can look up wastes turns. A role check should separate 'user must supply' from 'can be looked up'.

source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume? (arXiv 2603.26233 v3), results
finding: Gap 6 closed for resolve rates. A separate Intent Agent that only decides 'ask or not' beats a single agent told to check for ambiguity each turn, and matches an always-ask baseline. Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 500 SWE-bench Verified issues.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.5 resolve %: Full 70.8, Hidden 54.8, Interactive baseline (forced to ask) 70.4, UA-Single 61.2, UA-Multi 69.4. UA-Multi vs UA-Single p<0.001; vs Interactive p=0.621; vs Full p=0.458 (permutation tests). Kimi K2.6: UA-Multi 69.4 vs UA-Single 61.6 (p<0.001), Full 72.8 (gap p<0.05), Interactive only 47.2 (model used the finish tool to ask).
limits: Own Full baseline (70.8) is below the official OpenHands 74.2 (100 iterations vs 500). LLM user simulator. Two models only. 'No significant difference' on 500 items is weak evidence of equality.
agent_relevance: A decoupled gate that asks 'is something missing?' is worth more than the same question as an inline reminder (+8.2 points). Supports a separate missing-role check pass.

source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume?, calibration and cost
finding: UA-Multi asks selectively and costs more. For Sonnet 4.5 it queried in 344 tasks vs 369 for UA-Single, and where it asked it resolved 65.99% (UA-Single 55.81%, Hidden 44.48%). Where it did not ask it resolved 76.92% (Hidden 77.56%), so it skipped questions on tasks that were already solvable. The interactive baseline asked in nearly every task.
numbers: Mean queries per task, Sonnet 4.5: UA-Multi 3.06, UA-Single 1.84; Kimi K2.6 UA-Multi 8.71 (435 of 500 tasks asked, poorer calibration). Ask rate medium minus easy tasks: UA-Multi +9.28 points, UA-Single +2.43. Cost per task, Sonnet 4.5 (table text garbled; UA-Multi and UA-Single read as the last two values): about $3.50 vs $2.03; Kimi about $1.00 vs $0.65; paper says Multi is under double the single-agent cost.
limits: Row labels in the cost table did not survive PDF extraction; the cost mapping is inferred from the text 'less than double' and from order. Calibration differs by model (Kimi over-asks).
agent_relevance: Cost of the missing-role gate is about 1.5x to 1.7x per task for +8 points. No equal-token comparison was run, so this does not answer the equal-token question in gap 1.

source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume?, prompts used (Appendix B)
finding: Both gates use generic missing-information prompts, not role lists. UA-Single: reason explicitly about whether you have enough information, then write 'Ambiguity assessment: clear|ambiguous'. Intent Agent: asks what is the intended goal, what is missing, ambiguous or assumption-heavy, and what must be clarified before any action; outputs a boolean needs_clarification.
numbers: No condition compares a frame or role checklist with these generic prompts.
limits: So gap 2 (role check vs generic 'what is missing') is still untested directly.
agent_relevance: The Intent Agent's three questions are a light version of 'goal, missing slots, assumptions'. A role-list variant is a cheap ablation to add.

source: Hwang, Kim, Choi, Park, Lee (2026) Framing Matters / FRAGILE (arXiv 2605.28188)
finding: Gap 7 partly addressed. Fact-preserving reframing flips decisions often, and simple text-level prompts do not fix it; they can make it worse. Tested on Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B (main), plus GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-Flash-2.5-Lite and Llama-3.1-70B (appendix). A neutral re-framing step was not tested.
numbers: Abstract: average decision flip rate 28.6%. Value-tinted narration flip 36.3-47.2% vs paraphrase baseline 18.0-21.5% (7-8B models). Abstract: prompt-level and activation-level interventions fail to suppress framing sensitivity and actively amplify it; Llama value-anchor-only raises flips above base on temporal and vividness framings. Their representation-level method VALIGN cut Llama value-tinted flips 39.9% to 11.9%.
limits: The fix is a hidden-state intervention, so it needs open weights and does not transfer to an API agent. 2026 frontier models were not tested. Datasets are moral, medical, legal choice sets.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a one-line 'ignore framing' instruction works; measure flips. A neutral-restatement step (rewrite the task in plain terms, then answer) remains an open test.

finding: Closed small models show the same framing order (value-tinted > temporal > vividness). Gemini-Flash-2.5-Lite is less stable than GPT-4o-mini. Temporal framing on medical triage flips over 60% for both.
numbers: Average flip %: value-tinted GPT-4o-mini 30.5, Gemini 40.6; temporal 18.8 and 31.5; vividness 7.3 and 15.8.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity is not limited to 7B models, but frontier-model rates remain unmeasured here.

source: Kundi, Ahmad, Monahan (2026) FrameLLM for Requirements Generation (AAAI SuSS 2026)
finding: Gap 8 partly closed (c25 now read). The paper detects FrameNet frames in a requirement with spaCy and embeddings, then prompts the model with frame definitions and core and non-core frame elements and asks it to use all of them. It is a tiny study: five autonomous-driving requirements, each run three times, with small local Llama 3.2 models. Outcomes are counts and time plus qualitative remarks, not accuracy.
numbers: Requirement R01: baseline 7, 5, 7 requirements vs FrameLLM 44, 44, 44. R02: baseline 10, 10, 13 vs 26, 26, 26. Time R02 baseline 65 s, 65 s, 107 s vs 10-13 s.
limits: No human rating, no gold completeness, no equal-length control. More output is not more correct. Small models. Authors call results preliminary.
agent_relevance: Forcing every frame element into the output makes outputs longer and more stable. It does not show better answers. Not evidence for accuracy gains.

source: Jin et al. (2026) From Chat to Interview: OntoAgent (arXiv 2605.05828)
finding: Closest slot-checklist test for missing requirements. An ontology of requirement aspects, dimensions and slots chooses which slot to ask about next; the LLM only writes the question. It beat free-form prompting on ReqElicitGym (101 website scenarios).
numbers: IRE (implicit requirements elicited) / TKQR (early-question rate): Non-CoT 0.13/0.09; CoT 0.08/0.19; LLMREI-short 0.39/0.49; LLMREI-long 0.38/0.09; Mistake-guided prompt 0.52/0.48; OntoAgent 0.69/0.59 (+33% IRE, +21% TKQR over best baseline). Ablation on GPT-5.1: adding the ontology alone 0.13 to 0.41 IRE.
limits: The ontology is built from domain requirement text, not from FrameNet. Cost and tokens not compared. One domain (websites).
agent_relevance: A fixed slot checklist roughly tripled coverage over a plain prompt (0.13 to 0.41) on a current model. Indirect support for 'write the slots, find the blanks' and for gap 2: a slot list beat generic and mistake-guided prompts, though not at equal tokens.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Learning to Ask: When LLM Agents Meet Unclear Instruction (EMNLP 2025, NoisyToolBench, Ask-when-Needed)
finding: c26 now read. In 1000 real user queries, instructions missing key information were 56.0% of problematic ones (multiple references 11.3%, errors 17.3%, beyond tool capabilities 15.3%). Tool-calling agents tend to invent a missing argument. A prompt telling them to ask when blocked lifts the rate of asking an appropriate question (A1) a lot; A2 (correct API call) and A3 (final answer) gain less.
numbers: A1 on missing-info items with CoT then with AwN: gpt-4o 0.52 to 0.90; gpt-4 0.74 to 0.94; Claude 3.5 0.24 to 0.54; O3-mini 0.00 to 0.78; DeepSeek-R1 0.10 to 0.80. A3 on missing-info items: gpt-4o 0.34 to 0.36; Claude 3.5 0.20 to 0.50; o3-mini 0.16 to 0.52.
limits: Reasoning models almost never asked without the prompt (A1 0.00 to 0.10). Automatic evaluator is not fully accurate (paper's own limitation). Models are 2024-early 2025.
agent_relevance: Missing tool arguments are frame roles. Naming the blank is easy to induce with a prompt, but final-answer gains are small for some models, so the check must be followed by an actual ask or a flagged assumption.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu, van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Clarifying questions chosen by reasoning in the space of solutions (expected information gain) beat questions generated by reasoning only in question space. Tested with GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3 8B and 70B on a 20-questions animal task and on code generation (HumanEval, APPS) after eliciting 4 extra requirements.
numbers: Abstract-level claim read; per-model accuracies are in figures and tables that I did not transcribe. Not used as a number source.
limits: Older and small models. Efficiency measured in questions or test cases asked, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Ranking gaps by how much they narrow the answer set is better than a plain 'what is missing' list. This fits a step that scores each empty role.

source: Petruck (1996) Frame Semantics, Handbook of Pragmatics (summary of Fillmore 1975-1985)
finding: Gap 5 partly closed. A secondary review by a close colleague of Fillmore, covering the founding papers. The Commercial Transaction frame has buyer, seller, goods, money. Each verb brings some roles to the front and backgrounds others; backgrounded roles are optional and appear as oblique phrases. Interpreters invoke a frame to fill in what the text leaves out: a sentence about opening presents and blowing out candles invokes a birthday party with no mention of it.
numbers: No experiments with numbers. Qualitative examples only: buy focuses buyer and goods; sell focuses seller and goods; pay focuses buyer, money and seller. The land vs ground example: different words imply different background scenes.
quote: The words, that is, the linguistic material, evoke the frame
limits: Fillmore's own papers (1976, 1977, 1982, 1985) are still not read; this is a review. Fillmore ran no human experiments; the theory is argued from linguistic examples.
agent_relevance: Frames let the reader fill unstated roles from background knowledge. That is the failure mode to guard against: an agent filling blanks silently instead of flagging them.

source: Bower, Black, Turner (1979) Scripts in memory for text, Cognitive Psychology 11, 177-220
finding: Human evidence that readers fill missing script roles. From search-result summaries only: unstated script actions are confused with stated ones, and the confusion grows as more related script instances are read. Recognition ratings are highest for stated actions, intermediate for unstated script actions, lowest for novel false items.
numbers: No numbers obtained: the PDF returned HTTP 403 and a certificate error.
limits: Second-hand. A later citation (summary mention only) says recall of typical script actions was not significantly better than irrelevant information, so the script effect is bounded.
agent_relevance: Humans silently complete missing steps and later cannot tell inferred from stated. An agent should mark inferred fills as inferred.

finding: Negative result. Targeted web searches found no 2026 paper that reports per-role (means, instrument, cause) F1 for frontier models (GPT-5, Claude 4.x, Gemini 2.5 and later). The latest per-role numbers remain 2025 ones (Garat et al. Killing frame; Devasier et al.). The 2026 ACL short paper by Rai, Croce, Basili is fine-tuning on open Llama models.
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search; the Semantic Scholar, arXiv search and OpenAlex APIs returned 429 (rate limit), so a systematic query was not possible.
agent_relevance: Treat peripheral-role listing by frontier models as unmeasured. Our own pilot would have to measure it.

source: Search for a plain role-list control against FrameNet prompting (gap 4)
finding: Negative result. No study found that compares FrameNet-annotated prompts with a plain unlabelled role list or free-form slot list at equal tokens. The only control seen is the WordNet sense-tag variant in Iwamoto and Ohara (c15), which matched FrameNet. Kundi et al. (d10) compare only against a plain prompt.
numbers: None new. c15: GPT-4o-mini SWAG 75.2 base; FrameNet 79.5-80.3; WordNet 80.3.
limits: Iwamoto and Ohara was re-downloaded but not re-read this pass (Japanese text, garbled). Not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. The test has to be run by us: frame-labelled roles vs generic bullet slots vs nothing, at equal tokens.
